extracted.intended_audience: general readers; students and researchers of literature and Joseph Heller
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia biographical article about novelist Joseph Heller, summarizing his life, major works (notably Catch-22), themes, career history, and authorial practice. Useful for readers seeking background on Heller's genre, themes, and writing process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre classification
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article explicitly classifies Heller's work as satire and black comedy, indicating that his novels and other writings are intended to use humor (often dark or ironic) to critique society and institutions. Use this classification when situating or evaluating his work's tone and expected devices (irony, paradox, absurdity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Primary thematic focus (Catch-22)
rubrics_metrics.description: Catch-22 is described as 'a satire on war and bureaucracy, whose title has become a synonym for an absurd or contradictory choice.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating Catch-22 or Heller's related work, emphasize anti-war sentiment and critique of dehumanizing bureaucratic systems. The novel's central dilemmas, circular logic, and bureaucratic absurdities are core criteria for assessing whether a passage or plot element aligns with Heller's thematic aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broader thematic tendency
rubrics_metrics.description: Heller's other works are mostly modern satire which center on the lives of members of the middle class and often deliver anti-war or societal critique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess later novels and plays for satire aimed at middle-class mores, institutional critique, or existential/moral paradoxes rather than straightforward moralizing. Genre and target of satire are useful evaluative dimensions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creative-start practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Heller did not begin work on a story until he had envisioned both a first and last line. 'The first sentence usually appeared to him "independent of any conscious preparation."'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a descriptive rule of Heller's process: strong emphasis on memorable openings and planned endpoints. For emulating his method or analyzing his drafts, check whether the opening and closing function as deliberate bookends and whether openings appear syntactically/tonally distinct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate plotting and short-burst drafting
rubrics_metrics.description: Usually, within an hour or so of receiving his inspiration, Heller would have mapped out a basic plot and characters for the story. When ready to begin writing, he focused on one paragraph at a time, until he had three or four handwritten pages, which he then spent several hours reworking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate drafts or advise writers using this approach: prioritize rapid initial mapping of plot/characters, short concentrated bursts producing a few handwritten pages, followed by intensive immediate revision. This is a procedural guideline rather than a prescriptive aesthetic rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mid-project revision strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Only when he was almost one-third finished with the novel would he gain a clear vision of what it should be about. At that point, with the idea solidified, he would rewrite all that he had finished and then continue to the end of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This describes a staged revision tactic: expect substantial early rewriting when the overarching shape of the work becomes clear. For evaluating process or advising writers, treat early drafts as provisional and plan for a major restructuring roughly one-third into the project.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retention of original opening lines
rubrics_metrics.description: The finished version of the novel would often not begin or end with the sentences he had originally envisioned, although he usually tried to include the original opening sentence somewhere in the text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When studying Heller's texts or assessing drafts, look for displaced or repurposed original lines embedded later in the work — a characteristic of his revision habit that can signal continuity of inspiration even when order changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial stance / non-didactic philosophy
rubrics_metrics.description: Heller maintained that he did not 'have a philosophy of life, or a need to organize its progression. My books are not constructed to "say anything."'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This informs evaluation of thematic intent: avoid reading Heller as preaching a fixed moral or constructing explicit philosophical arguments; instead, prioritize tone, irony, and depiction of absurdity. Critiques should focus on representation and satirical technique rather than asserted authorial doctrine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication and reception trajectory as success metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Catch-22 received mixed initial reviews and modest hardback sales (30,000 copies first year) but later became widely popular (10 million US sales) and entered canonical lists (Modern Library top 100).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use both contemporaneous critical reception and long-term cultural impact/sales when assessing a work's significance. Early negative reviews do not preclude eventual canonical status; pedagogical adoption (e.g., by institutions) and linguistic penetration (title becoming a common term) are also signals of impact.
